clue.text: Brief, displaying discretion

definitions.note: the clue word is a singular noun; the answer is its plural equivalent, a set of instructions

indicators.note: to display is to lay out on show, so the letters are set out in a fresh arrangement

parts.note: taken as written, ten letters to rearrange

explanation.walkthrough: 'Brief' looks like an adjective meaning short, but here it is the noun: a lawyer's or agent's brief is a set of instructions. The ten letters of 'discretion' rearrange to DIRECTIONS.
explanation.definitionFit: A brief is the instructions given to someone for a task, which are the orders or guidance they must follow.

clue.text: See what you can get from a palm tree

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to go out with someone romantically

definitions.text: what you can get from a palm tree
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the sweet brown fruit of a particular palm

explanation.surface: An invitation to look at what a palm tree yields.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' reads as an imperative to look, but it is a verb meaning to court someone, as in 'are you seeing anyone?'.
explanation.definitionFit: To be romantically involved with someone is to go out with them; separately, the palm fruit is a sticky brown sweet fruit.

clue.text: Money in imperialism

indicators.note: something sitting inside a word can be read straight out of its letters

parts.note: the fifth to eighth letters of this word

explanation.surface: Wealth gathered through empire-building.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the riches of empire, but the currency sits inside the word itself: impeRIALism.
explanation.definitionFit: The rial is the currency unit of Iran, Oman and Yemen, so it is a form of money.

clue.text: Better nominate extraordinary explorer

parts.note: to cap something is to better or outdo it

indicators.note: something extraordinary is out of the ordinary, so these letters leave their usual order

parts.note: taken as written, eight letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A recommendation to put forward a remarkable explorer for some honour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' looks like an adjective but is the verb to cap, as in capping a story with a better one. Captain Nemo commands the submarine Nautilus in Jules Verne's Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Verne's submarine captain roams the world's oceans charting unknown depths, making him a fictional underwater explorer.

clue.text: Everyman shall pass on acrimony

parts.note: the setter speaks of himself as 'I', so 'Everyman shall' is I'LL with the apostrophe dropped
to will property is to pass it on to an heir

explanation.surface: The setter declares he will hand down bitterness to his heirs.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's pseudonym stands for 'I', a common crossword convention. 'Pass on' reads as one phrase, but 'pass' alone is the verb to bequeath and 'on' just links it to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Acrimony is bitter hostility between people, which is the same as resentful animosity or bad feeling.

clue.text: Fools childminders (independent, not amateur)

indicators.note: putting one thing in place of another, 'X, not Y', tells you to swap the second out for the first

parts.note: nannies look after other people's children
I is the standard abbreviation for independent
A is the abbreviation for amateur

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses a group of nannies as idiots, with an aside about who is self-employed and who is professional.
explanation.walkthrough: In the word for childminders, the A is replaced by I, giving NINNIES.
explanation.definitionFit: A ninny is a silly, foolish person, so the plural noun matches a group of idiots or simpletons.

clue.text: At the outset, 'Terrible' sort; aristocratic Russian!

definitions.text: At the outset, 'Terrible' sort; aristocratic Russian

indicators.note: the outset is the very start, so only the opening letter of each following word counts

parts.note: the opening letters of these four words

explanation.surface: A description of an aristocratic Russian of the 'Terrible' kind, like Ivan.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: its initials spell the answer, and 'Terrible' sort points to Ivan the Terrible, the first ruler crowned with this title.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivan the Terrible was the first crowned emperor of Russia, so a 'Terrible' sort of aristocratic Russian is a Russian monarch.

clue.text: It has white and brown meat, bird cooked with capers

definitions.text: It has white and brown meat

indicators.note: cooking transforms ingredients, so these letters are worked into a new form

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A recipe description: a bird with white and brown meat, cooked with capers.
explanation.walkthrough: White and brown meat suggests poultry, which the word 'bird' reinforces, but the creature is a shellfish; crabs yield white claw meat and brown body meat.
explanation.definitionFit: This long-legged crab, like other edible crabs, provides both white meat from the legs and brown meat from inside the shell.

clue.text: Stern seller sent bananas

indicators.note: going bananas means going crazy, so these letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written, ten letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A strict shopkeeper ships off a load of bananas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bananas' looks like the goods being sent, but it is slang for crazy and tells you to rearrange 'seller sent'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone stern is severe and unyielding, which matches being harsh and unwilling to ease off or show mercy.

clue.text: Heavily stomp over boundary where sportsperson may jump

parts.note: to tramp is to walk with heavy steps
O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over
a line marks a boundary

explanation.surface: An athlete stamps over the boundary line, perhaps a long jumper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' looks like a preposition but supplies O, the abbreviation for a cricket over (a set of six balls).
explanation.definitionFit: Trampolining is an Olympic gymnastics event, and the sprung frame is the place on which its athletes bounce.

clue.text: Laid back? Don't touch that… !

definitions.note: fill in the blank: the answer completes the catchphrase

indicators.note: going back means going backwards, so the letters are read from right to left

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A relaxed person tells others not to touch something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Laid back' reads as relaxed, but it splits into the word and an instruction to reverse it. The ellipsis invites you to finish the old broadcasting catchphrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Radio and television presenters once said 'don't touch that dial' to stop listeners tuning away during a break.

clue.text: Following calm, canoe lost in vast watery expanse

indicators.note: coming after something means being placed straight behind it in the line

parts.note: pacific means peaceful or calm

indicators.note: something lost has gone astray, so these letters wander from their usual order

parts.note: taken as written, five letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: After a period of calm, a canoe goes missing on a huge stretch of water.
explanation.walkthrough: The ocean was named 'Pacific' by Magellan because its waters seemed calm, so the clue's surface and wordplay overlap neatly.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the largest of Earth's oceans, covering about a third of the planet's surface, a truly huge body of sea.

clue.text: Watching from above … or not noticing at all?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: having a view down onto something, as a window does a garden
second meaning: failing to see or ignoring something

explanation.walkthrough: The one word carries two nearly opposite senses: looking down on something closely, and missing it entirely.
explanation.definitionFit: A house can have a view over a valley, and a careless reader can miss an error; the same participle covers both.

clue.text: Was divisive, perhaps premeditated

definitions.meaning: first meaning: did sums such as division, playfully rendered as being 'divisive'
second meaning: planned in advance, deliberate

explanation.surface: Someone caused division, possibly on purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Divisive' suggests causing discord, but read literally it means doing division, one example of working out figures; 'perhaps' flags that example.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing division is one kind of arithmetic working-out, and a deliberate, planned crime is described as cold and intentional in the same word.

clue.text: This is one of those tirades

definitions.note: the clue's 'this' is one instance; the answer names the plural class
definitions.meaning: first meaning: the puzzle you are solving belongs to this kind of thing
second meaning: angry words, split as two words

explanation.surface: A remark that something is a typical example of an outburst.
explanation.walkthrough: The self-referential 'This' means the puzzle itself; 'tirades' is read as two words, angry ones.
explanation.definitionFit: The puzzle in your hand is an instance of the grid-based word game, and tirades are bitter, angry exchanges of speech.

clue.text: A doctor, way back, that's describing a gland

parts.note: taken as written
Dr is the title abbreviation for doctor

indicators.note: going back means travelling backwards, so the letters run right to left

parts.note: a lane is a narrow road or way

explanation.surface: A medic, some time ago, giving an account of a gland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Way back' reads as 'long ago', but 'way' supplies a road and 'back' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective names the pair of glands sitting above the kidneys, so it is a word used to describe that gland.

clue.text: $10,149 for Banksy piece?

parts.note: the dollar sign is a stylised letter S
the number written out as a word
a loose Roman numeral: C is 100 and IL is 49 (strictly 149 is CXLIX)

explanation.surface: A price tag of $10,149 on an artwork by Banksy.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma makes it look like one sum of money, but it splits into three pieces read three different ways: symbol, word and Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: Banksy, the anonymous British street artist, makes much of his graffiti by spraying paint through cut-out templates; the question mark marks it as an example.

clue.text: Perhaps change revolted expression on initially seeing nibbles

parts.note: loose change is an example of money in coins
'ew' is what you say when disgusted

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of the next word is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of this word

explanation.surface: Someone's face changes to disgust on first seeing the snacks offered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolted' suggests a reversal, but here it means disgusted, and the disgusted exclamation is simply 'ew'.
explanation.definitionFit: Nibbles are small savoury snacks served with drinks, and bowls of these kidney-shaped nuts are a typical example.

clue.text: Ultimately, Marge's troublemaker lad?

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter of the next word is kept

parts.note: the final letter of this word
an imp is a mischievous child
a lad can be someone's son

explanation.surface: A question about Marge's mischievous boy.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also defines: Marge's troublemaking son is Bart, of the cartoon family whose surname is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Bart, the mischief-making eldest child of Marge and Homer in the long-running cartoon, bears this family surname.

clue.text: At sea, Sea Lord primes weaponry again

indicators.note: to be at sea is to be confused and lost, so these letters are muddled

parts.note: taken as written, seven letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A senior naval officer readies the ship's guns while out at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At sea' fits the naval scene as a location but signals confusion. A Sea Lord is a senior officer on the British Admiralty Board.
explanation.definitionFit: To charge guns afresh with ammunition after firing is to make weapons ready once more for use.

clue.text: Drink some clarets inappropriately

indicators.note: some means a part of what follows, so the letters are a run taken from within the words

parts.note: runs across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Someone drinking claret at the wrong time or in the wrong place.
explanation.walkthrough: The wine sits across the words: claRETS INAppropriately.
explanation.definitionFit: Retsina is a Greek white wine flavoured with pine resin, so it is an alcoholic beverage.

clue.text: Two moons fail to display Newtonian principles

indicators.note: something that fails breaks down, so these letters collapse into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, and also doing double duty as the signal

explanation.surface: Two moons that fail to obey the rules of physics Newton set down.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram fodder is 'Two moons fail', and 'fail' both joins the fodder and signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Isaac Newton set out three rules describing how bodies move under forces, and they are known by this collective name.

clue.text: Lead actor that's over 8 on board?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the principal performer in a film or play
second meaning: the asterisk symbol printed above the 8 on a keyboard

explanation.walkthrough: '8' looks like a cross-reference to 8 down, and 'on board' suggests a ship; the board is a keyboard, where the asterisk shares the 8 key.
explanation.definitionFit: The principal performer gets top billing, and the asterisk symbol on a standard keyboard's eight key is commonly called by this name.

clue.text: The French rehashed gutted calorific ingredient

parts.note: la is the French feminine word for 'the'

indicators.note: a gutted thing has its insides removed, leaving only its outer shell

parts.note: the first and last letters of this word

explanation.surface: A fattening ingredient that the French serve up again in a reworked dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rehashed' is not a signal here but the word to be emptied: 'gutted' strips it to its outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: This rendered pig fat is used in cooking and baking and is very high in calories, so it fattens any dish.

clue.text: Heard, in short walk, an aquatic bird

indicators.note: what is heard is taken by the ear, so the spoken form matters, not the spelling

parts.note: to take a turn is to go for a short stroll

explanation.surface: Something overheard during a brief stroll, about a water bird.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'turn' round the garden or the park is a British way of saying a short stroll.
explanation.definitionFit: Terns are slender seabirds related to gulls, living by and feeding from the sea, so they are water birds.

clue.text: Eccentric star is paid with indoor plant

indicators.note: eccentric means off-centre and odd, so these letters are knocked out of their order

parts.note: taken as written, ten letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: An oddball celebrity gets paid in houseplants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eccentric star' reads as a quirky celebrity, but 'Eccentric' is the signal and 'star is paid' the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The aspidistra is a hardy leafy plant famous as a Victorian parlour plant that thrives indoors in poor light.

clue.text: Retired horse unhappy to race

indicators.note: retiring means withdrawing or going back, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: horse is slang for heroin, abbreviated H
sad means unhappy

explanation.surface: A racehorse put out to grass is miserable at no longer running.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retired horse' suggests an old racehorse, but 'Retired' reverses the whole of 'horse unhappy'; H for heroin, nicknamed horse, is a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: To race is to rush or hurry somewhere at speed, so the verbs mean the same thing.

clue.text: Compromised? Stop seething

parts.note: to end something is to stop it
someone seething is very angered

explanation.surface: Someone agrees to a deal and is told to stop fuming about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Compromised' suggests settling a dispute, but it means put at risk, as in compromising someone's safety.
explanation.definitionFit: Something whose safety has been compromised is put in danger or under threat, the sense used of at-risk species.
